adds.title: LGBTQ rights in Indonesia - Wikipedia
adds.summary: Wikipedia's country overview (LGBTQ rights in Indonesia) documents the national framework a visitor to Bengkulu stands under: consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised in private but there are no anti-discrimination protections for LGBT people, the 2022 penal-code amendment criminalising sex outside marriage takes effect on 2 January 2026 (up to one year in prison, actionable on a complaint by an immediate family member), and legal gender recognition requires sex-reassignment surgery plus a judge's approval. The page also records Indonesia's votes against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2016, 2022 and 2025; police raids on a private-villa gathering described as a 'gay party' (22 June 2025) and the 11 August 2025 arrest of three men over a Facebook community page; and a 2025 Pew survey in which 93% of Indonesians rated homosexuality morally unacceptable. These dated, independently corroborating national specifics ground the record's at-national-score risk assessment for Bengkulu: no province-specific protection, ordinance or incident was documented for Bengkulu itself.

adds.title: LGBTQ rights in Indonesia - Wikipedia
adds.summary: Wikipedia's country overview (LGBTQ rights in Indonesia) supplies the national framework Jambi is assessed under: same-sex conduct is not criminalised in private but LGBT people have no anti-discrimination protections, the 2022 penal-code amendment criminalising extramarital sex enters force on 2 January 2026 with up to one year's imprisonment on an immediate-family complaint, and legal gender recognition is conditioned on sex-reassignment surgery plus judicial approval. The page further records Indonesia's 2016, 2022 and 2025 votes against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, police raids on a 'gay party' at a private villa (22 June 2025), the 11 August 2025 arrest of three men over an LGBTQ Facebook community page, and a 2025 Pew survey finding 93% of Indonesians view homosexuality as morally unacceptable. These dated national specifics corroborate and sharpen the record's 'national climate' assessment for Jambi, where no local ordinance, protection or documented incident was found in either direction.
